protocol.instrument_name: NSW Pharmacist Practice Standards for Management of Herpes Zoster
protocol.instrument_version: NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026); approved 28 August 2026 by Dr Kerry Chant AO PSM, Chief Health Officer and Deputy Secretary Population and Public Health
protocol.legal_basis: NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026). Pharmacists must hold general registration under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law and have successfully completed the training requirements detailed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026). Approved Medicines are listed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026).
protocol.supervision_model: approved pharmacist - for appropriately trained approved pharmacists to manage eligible patients as part of the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026); 'Pharmacists must exercise professional discretion and judgement when applying the information within these Practice Standards.'
protocol.scope_summary: NSW Health practice standard for approved pharmacists managing eligible patients (aged 18 years or older) with herpes zoster (shingles) under the Community Pharmacy Herpes Zoster Service: three approved oral antivirals (Valaciclovir, Famciclovir, Aciclovir), patient assessment flowchart, informed consent, eligibility and urgent referral criteria, up to 10 days of oral therapy before referral, antiviral window within 72 hours of rash onset, 48-72 hour clinical review, transmission precautions, zoster vaccination advice, documentation and communication requirements.

inclusion.text: Patients must be aged 18 years or older to be eligible for the service.

provenance.section_heading: G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA

inclusion.text: Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of herpes zoster.
The patient has no red flags, or exclusions (checked against Section G, Patient eligibility and referral criteria).
Informed clinical and financial consent must be obtained from the patient prior to providing care under these Practice Standards.
Patients must be physically present in the pharmacy to be eligible for management.
Patients are required to have a consultation with an approved pharmacist before a medication can be supplied under the Authority.
To receive management for herpes zoster under this service, the patient must fulfill the eligibility requirements set out under Part G of the Practice Standards.

G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA

steps.description: Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of herpes zoster.

Is the patient >=18 years old? If No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to Check Section G (Patient eligibility and referral criteria) to determine if patient may be treated and/or must be referred for GP or ED management.'

Does the patient have any red flags, or exclusions? If Yes: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to Check Section G (Patient eligibility and referral criteria) to determine if patient may be treated and/or must be referred for GP or ED management.'

gates.criterion: No red flags and no exclusions under Section G

steps.description: Obtain informed consent: Participation; Financial; Pharmacist communication with other health practitioners. If No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to Check Section G (Patient eligibility and referral criteria) to determine if patient may be treated and/or must be referred for GP or ED management.'

gates.criterion: Informed consent obtained (participation, financial, pharmacist communication with other health practitioners)

steps.description: Conduct patient history and clinical review including review of contraindications, precautions, drug interactions, pregnancy and lactation status.
Establish management plan.
Communicate agreed management plan with patient and patient's medical practitioner. Document all aspects of management plan.

Sufficient information must be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of management. The My Health Record should be reviewed where appropriate and available. The patient history should include: Age; Pregnancy and lactation status (if applicable).

The patient history should include (continued): Nature, sensitivity and frequency of symptoms; Nature of rash (distribution, appearance, number of lesions); Onset and duration of symptoms; Precipitating and relieving factors; History of VZV infection; Underlying medical conditions including: immunocompromise, auto-immune diseases, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, HIV, cancer, conditions treated with immunosuppressant or immunomodulator therapies (including corticosteroids), renal impairment, transplant recipients, chronic lung conditions; Current medications (including prescribed medications, vitamins, herbs, other supplements and over-the-counter medications); Medication and other strategies used to treat current symptoms; Drug allergies/adverse drug events; Immunisation status as per the Australian Immunisation Handbook (AIH) (herpes zoster and varicella vaccinations).
Examination of the rash and documentation of its characteristics and location, as well as any signs of complication. Exclusion of other conditions with similar presentation.

Laboratory confirmation is generally not required for typical presentations and uncomplicated cases of herpes zoster. Confirmatory pathology testing (initiated by a medical practitioner) is required for cases where diagnosis is uncertain, when complicated disease is a possibility, or in cases of herpes zoster in people who have been previously vaccinated against herpes zoster.

gates.criterion: Diagnosis is uncertain, complicated disease is a possibility, or herpes zoster occurs in a person previously vaccinated against herpes zoster

steps.description: Patients with signs or symptoms of eye involvement require urgent review by a medical practitioner.

gates.criterion: No signs or symptoms of eye involvement

steps.description: If the rash has presented for more than 72 hours, antiviral therapy is not recommended and will usually self-resolve in low-risk patients.

gates.criterion: Rash presented within 72 hours of first appearance of the rash

steps.description: Antiviral treatment can reduce acute pain, duration of the rash, viral shedding and ocular complications if commenced within 72 hours of the first appearance of the rash but is not indicated in all patients.

Antiviral therapy is indicated for the following group: All patients who present within 72 hours of onset of the rash as outlined in section G of the Practice Standards should be provided with antiviral therapy. Antiviral therapy in accordance with Therapeutic Guidelines: Shingles.

gates.criterion: Patient presents within 72 hours of onset of the rash

steps.description: Antiviral therapy is indicated regardless of the time elapsed since onset of rash for: Immunocompromised patients (including those with HIV infection) - these patients require urgent referral to a medical practitioner; Patients with herpes zoster ophthalmicus regardless of time lapsed from rash onset - these patients require urgent referral to a medical practitioner.

gates.criterion: Immunocompromised patient (including those with HIV infection) or patient with herpes zoster ophthalmicus

steps.description: Supportive management: Education and advice regarding care for lesions: use of dressings, cleaning and appropriate clothing. Education and advice regarding transmission precautions in accordance with Healthdirect: Shingles.

Pharmacotherapy: Antiviral therapy in accordance with Therapeutic Guidelines: Shingles. Analgesia for mild nociceptive shingles pain within normal over-the-counter pharmacist scope of practice. All patients requiring more substantial analgesia, presenting with neuropathic pain, or presenting with moderate to severe nociceptive pain require a referral to a medical practitioner.

gates.criterion: Mild nociceptive shingles pain manageable within normal over-the-counter pharmacist scope of practice

steps.description: Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, and other relevant references should be provided to the patient regarding: Medicine use (e.g. dosing); How to manage side effects; Recommendations for vaccination against herpes zoster; When to seek further care and/or treatment, including recognising superinfection and herpes zoster complications; When to return to the pharmacist for a review.

The agreed management plan must be documented in the patient electronic clinical record and shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary team, in accordance with the Authority. Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

All patients should be advised to contact a medical practitioner if: They are not responding to treatment; Their signs and symptoms worsen; They are experiencing complications (as soon as they become evident); They are having unmanageable adverse effects.

Preventing transmission: The patient should be advised to inform any high-risk contacts (pregnant women, neonates in the first month of life and immunocompromised individuals) who have had significant exposure to a person with active VZV (household contacts or where there has been direct face-to-face contact for 5 minutes or being within the same roof for at least an hour) to seek medical care as soon as possible. People with herpes zoster are infectious from 1-2 days prior to the onset of the rash, until vesicles have dried and scabbed (usually 5 days after the onset of the rash). Rashes should be covered with appropriate dressings until the patient is no longer infectious and contact with pregnant women, neonates, and immunocompromised people must be avoided.

Zoster vaccination: Vaccination against herpes zoster is the best way to prevent herpes zoster and reduce the risk of complications but is not indicated during an acute herpes zoster episode or to treat PHN. People who have had a previous episode of herpes zoster can be vaccinated against a recurrence; the interval between the episode and vaccination is dependent on the patient's immune status. Refer to the Australian Immunisation Handbook for herpes zoster information and recommendations. The optimal age to be vaccinated against herpes zoster and the vaccine type will differ based on immune status, duration of protection of chosen vaccine and the individual's choice.

gates.criterion: Vaccination not during an acute herpes zoster episode and not to treat PHN

steps.description: Clinical review with the pharmacist should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines.
Patients should be advised and educated on how and when to seek a review with medical practitioner.

If a patient experiences worsening of symptoms, minimal improvement in symptoms after commencing pharmacist care, or onset of herpes zoster complications, they must be referred for an urgent review by a medical practitioner.

gates.criterion: No worsening of symptoms, improvement in symptoms after commencing pharmacist care, and no onset of herpes zoster complications

steps.description: A clinical review is recommended 48-72 hours after the initial presentation to assess for: Progression of the rash; The clinical signs or symptoms of herpes zoster; Screening for complications of herpes zoster; Adverse effects of therapy.
The pharmacist must make an electronic clinical record, and a record in a pharmacy dispensing system regarding the supply of any medications under these services, in accordance with the Authority.
Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

red_flags.trigger_text: When the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal cranial nerve is affected (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) ... Vesicles on the nose have been found to be predictive of eye involvement (Hutchinson sign) and suggest herpes zoster ophthalmicus. The condition is considered an ophthalmologic emergency due to the risk of vision loss if not quickly identified and treated early in the disease course. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department or eye hospital for urgent medical assessment.

Complications occur in approximately 13 to 26% of patients with herpes zoster and are most prevalent in older people and those who are immunocompromised. Caution must be exercised by pharmacists managing patients with suspected complex presentations and complications of herpes zoster. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients for urgent medical assessment at presentation or at any stage if a complication develops.

Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN): neuropathic pain that persists for at least 90 days after the onset of the rash or re-occurs; sharp/shooting and intermittent, described as constant burning, often with extreme sensitivity to touch (allodynia). These patients require referral to a medical practitioner for review and management of pain.

Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: suggested by tearing, ocular pain, blurred vision, conjunctival infection, swelling/erythema of the lid and periorbital structures, uveitis, episcleritis, keratitis. Vesicles on the nose have been found to be predictive of eye involvement. The condition is considered an ophthalmologic emergency due to the risk of vision loss if not quickly identified and treated early in the disease course. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment.

Acute retinal necrosis: clinical features include acute iridocyclitis, vitritis, necrotizing retinitis, occlusive retinal vasculitis with rapid loss of vision, and eventual retinal detachment. The condition is considered an ophthalmologic emergency due to the risk of vision loss if not quickly identified and treated early in the disease course. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment.

Disseminated zoster (VZV dissemination): whilst most individuals have some lesions external to the primary dermatome, disseminated zoster is defined as 20 or more lesions outside of the dermatome and may be clinically indistinguishable from varicella infection. Viral dissemination to the central nervous system and viscera (lungs, gut, liver and brain) may occur.

Disseminated zoster suggested by: >2 contiguous dermatomes, bilateral involvement [lesions crossing the midline], involvement of non-contiguous dermatomes, visceral involvement. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment.
Secondary bacterial skin infections (referral to a medical practitioner for swab and culture is required).

Pregnant women who are exposed to VZV (chicken pox or herpes zoster) for the first time (no or uncertain history of previous chicken pox infection) may develop chicken pox which can have serious consequences, including maternal mortality and morbidity, foetal varicella syndrome and the associated abnormalities. Urgent referral to an emergency department is required as zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) should be given to all seronegative women within 96 hours (4 days).
Patients with signs or symptoms of eye involvement require urgent review by a medical practitioner.
Immunocompromised patients (including those with HIV infection) regardless of the time elapsed since onset of rash. These patients require urgent referral to a medical practitioner.
Patients with herpes zoster ophthalmicus regardless of time lapsed from rash onset. These patients require urgent referral to a medical practitioner.
All patients requiring more substantial analgesia, presenting with neuropathic pain, or presenting with moderate to severe nociceptive pain require a referral to a medical practitioner.

All patients should be advised to contact a medical practitioner if: They are not responding to treatment; Their signs and symptoms worsen; They are experiencing complications (as soon as they become evident); They are having unmanageable adverse effects.

If a patient experiences worsening of symptoms, minimal improvement in symptoms after commencing pharmacist care, or onset of herpes zoster complications, they must be referred for an urgent review by a medical practitioner.

If the treating pharmacist becomes aware of an uncommon, unexpected or serious adverse event following treatment with an Approved Medicine, this should be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration. This should be conducted via the usual processes, by reporting online at https://aems.tga.gov.au/. Additionally, you must notify the patient's usual general practitioner (if they have one).

routine: Patients who have requested the service but are not eligible for management should be referred to their regular medical practitioner or health service.

Patients who meet any of the urgent referral criteria below must be referred to their regular medical practitioner, maternity provider, health service, or Emergency Department (ED) as indicated in the table. Note that these are not exhaustive lists.
Pharmacists must apply clinical judgement and refer any patient considered appropriate for medical care.
These patients require referral to a medical practitioner for review and management of pain. (postherpetic neuralgia)
Secondary bacterial skin infections (referral to a medical practitioner for swab and culture is required).

All patients should be advised to contact a medical practitioner if: They are not responding to treatment; Their signs and symptoms worsen; They are experiencing complications (as soon as they become evident); They are having unmanageable adverse effects.
urgent: Urgent: ED* (Pregnancy) - *Pharmacist to phone ED with notice of urgent medical referral. Patient must be advised not to attend a maternity or antenatal ward/appointment while symptoms are present.

Urgent: ED - The patient does not respond to one course of optimal therapy or condition worsens; Diagnosis is uncertain; Antiviral treatment is indicated but the patient is allergic to valaciclovir, acyclovir and/or famciclovir; Multi-dermatomal rash; Disseminated zoster; Atypical cutaneous presentation; Complications of herpes zoster.
Urgent: GP - The patient is aged under 18 years of age; Previous vaccination for herpes zoster; Neuropathic shingle pain or moderate-to-severe nociceptive pain.

Urgent: ED or GP - Immunocompromised patients (due to underlying medical condition or due to medication taken by the patient). Urgent: ED or eye hospital (for suspicions of herpes zoster ophthalmicus or acute retinal necrosis) - Herpes zoster affecting the face, eyes, genitals.

Patients with signs or symptoms of eye involvement require urgent review by a medical practitioner. Immunocompromised patients (including those with HIV infection) and patients with herpes zoster ophthalmicus require urgent referral to a medical practitioner.

If a patient experiences worsening of symptoms, minimal improvement in symptoms after commencing pharmacist care, or onset of herpes zoster complications, they must be referred for an urgent review by a medical practitioner.
emergency: Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department or eye hospital for urgent medical assessment. (herpes zoster ophthalmicus)
Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients for urgent medical assessment at presentation or at any stage if a complication develops. (complications of herpes zoster)
Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment. (herpes zoster ophthalmicus; acute retinal necrosis; disseminated zoster)

review_followup.when: If patients are not responding to treatment, signs and symptoms worsen, complications occur (as soon as they become evident), or unmanageable adverse effects

conditions: If the treating pharmacist becomes aware of an uncommon, unexpected or serious adverse event following treatment with an Approved Medicine, this should be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration. This should be conducted via the usual processes, by reporting online at https://aems.tga.gov.au/.
Additionally, you must notify the patient's usual general practitioner (if they have one).
Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

The pharmacist must seek the patient's consent to share a record of the consultation and any subsequent consultations (including adverse events) with the patient's usual treating medical practitioner or medical practice, where the patient has one. If the patient consents to the disclosure, the record must be shared within a week following the consultation.

open_questions.topic: No strengths, forms beyond 'oral', doses, routes, frequencies or durations printed for valaciclovir, famciclovir and aciclovir
open_questions.observed: The three Approved Medicines (valaciclovir (oral), famciclovir (oral), aciclovir (oral)) are listed by name and route only; dosing detail is deferred to 'Antiviral therapy in accordance with Therapeutic Guidelines: Shingles' (p11) and the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026).
open_questions.why_unclear: form (oral) and route (oral) were transcribed from the Approved Medicines list; strength, dose, frequency, duration and max_dose were left empty rather than invented.

open_questions.topic: No first-line designation among the three approved antivirals
open_questions.observed: Valaciclovir (oral), Famciclovir (oral) and Aciclovir (oral) are listed alphabetically with no ranking; pharmacotherapy is directed to the Therapeutic Guidelines: Shingles.
open_questions.why_unclear: first_line set to false for all treatments; no agent is designated first-line in the document.

open_questions.topic: Flowchart box order reconstructed from interleaved diagram layout
open_questions.observed: Section D flowchart text is interleaved, e.g. 'Is the patient >=18 years old? No under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to ... Yes ... Check Section G (Patient eligibility and referral criteria) to determine if patient may be treated and/or must be referred for GP or ED management.' with Yes/No branch labels detached from boxes.
open_questions.why_unclear: Step order and on_fail assignments were inferred from the diagram layout; branch wording transcribed verbatim. Confidence medium on PW-1-S2 and PW-1-S3.

open_questions.topic: Mirrored/reversed text rendered in the Section G table area
open_questions.observed: Page 5 extraction shows reversed text 'sngis gninraw 'gafl deR'' (i.e. 'Red flag' warning signs) immediately after the 'Page 5 of 16' footer and above the table rows, plus the table header printed as 'Referral criteria Treat Referral'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Likely a rotated/overlaid element in the PDF; the table heading could not be read reliably, so table rows were attributed to the section heading 'G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA'.

open_questions.topic: Table rows marked Treat: Yes also carry Urgent referral destinations
open_questions.observed: Eight referral-criteria rows are marked 'Treat: Yes' yet specify 'Urgent: ED', 'Urgent: GP' or 'Urgent: ED or GP' (immunocompromised, multi-dermatomal rash, disseminated zoster, atypical cutaneous presentation, face/eyes/genitals, complications, previous vaccination, neuropathic or moderate-to-severe pain), while the preamble says pharmacists must not provide management where there is a 'No' in the 'Treat' column.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not state whether the pharmacist may supply treatment while simultaneously making the urgent referral for 'Yes' rows; both the Treat value and the referral destination were transcribed as printed and the rows captured as red flags with confidence medium.

open_questions.observed: Approved Medicines lists 'Aciclovir (oral)' (p2) while the allergy referral row prints 'allergic to valaciclovir, acyclovir and/or famciclovir' (p5).
open_questions.why_unclear: Both spellings transcribed verbatim; they appear to refer to the same medicine but the document does not reconcile them.

open_questions.topic: 'Higher quantity as specified in the Authority' not printed
open_questions.observed: 'Pharmacists can supply up to 10 days of oral therapy before referring a patient to a medical practitioner, or a higher quantity as specified in the Authority.' (p4)
open_questions.why_unclear: The higher quantity is held in the external NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026) and is not printed here; quantity_to_supply records the 10-day limit verbatim.

open_questions.topic: 72-hour antiviral window vs 'regardless of time' groups
open_questions.observed: 'If the rash has presented for more than 72 hours, antiviral therapy is not recommended and will usually self-resolve in low-risk patients' (p7), while 'Immunocompromised patients (including those with HIV infection) regardless of the time elapsed since onset of rash' and 'Patients with herpes zoster ophthalmicus regardless of time lapsed from rash onset' are indicated groups (p10).
open_questions.why_unclear: Both readings recorded: PW-3-S1 gate routes a >72-hour presentation to PW-3-S4 (regardless-of-time groups), and PW-3-S4 stops antiviral therapy for patients outside those groups. The document does not print this branch explicitly.

open_questions.topic: Referral and eligibility statements span multiple pages
open_questions.observed: referral.routine quotes from pages 4, 5, 8, 9 and 11; urgent from pages 5, 10 and 12; emergency from pages 7, 8, 9. The Section G table itself spans pages 5-6.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance object for the referral block using the first page; page range recorded here.

open_questions.topic: Referral criteria lists stated as not exhaustive
open_questions.observed: 'Note that these are not exhaustive lists.' and 'Pharmacists must apply clinical judgement and refer any patient considered appropriate for medical care.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The red-flag and exclusion lists cannot be treated as complete; the engine must allow pharmacist-initiated referral for any reason.

open_questions.topic: Previous vaccination for herpes zoster: Treat: Yes with Urgent: GP
open_questions.observed: The Section G table marks 'Previous vaccination for herpes zoster' as Treat: Yes with Referral: Urgent: GP (p6), while examination requires confirmatory pathology testing for 'herpes zoster in people who have been previously vaccinated against herpes zoster' (p10) and vaccination advice says people with a previous episode can be vaccinated (p12).
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not explain how a previously vaccinated patient can be managed by the pharmacist if an urgent GP referral is required at eligibility check; both statements recorded as printed.

open_questions.observed: 'Photophobia (approximately 80% of cases).' is listed as a prodromal symptom bullet without stating 80% of what population (prodromal cases, all cases, or another denominator).
open_questions.why_unclear: Qualifier ambiguous in source; transcribed verbatim and not converted into a structured rule.

open_questions.topic: Notifiable and documentation conditions span pages 2, 4, 11 and 13
open_questions.observed: TGA adverse event reporting and GP notification wording is on page 2; consent record sharing within a week is on page 4; My Health Record upload requirement appears on pages 11 and 13.
open_questions.why_unclear: Shared provenance uses the first page (2) per spec; page range recorded here.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Verify the current NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026) Approved Medicines list, including formulations and strengths for valaciclovir, famciclovir and aciclovir, and any subsequent amendments.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The Approved Medicines list (with formulations/strengths) is held in an external Authority document not included in this protocol PDF; no strengths are printed here.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm each pharmacist using the module has completed the training requirements detailed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026) and holds general registration under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Training requirements are detailed in an external document; pharmacist authorisation to practise under the standard must be verified locally.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local process for TGA adverse event reporting via https://aems.tga.gov.au/ and notification of the patient's usual general practitioner.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Reporting is directed to be done 'via the usual processes', which is left to local policy.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm permitted supply quantities: 'up to 10 days of oral therapy' versus 'a higher quantity as specified in the Authority'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The higher quantity is defined in the external Authority and is not printed in this document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm consent record-sharing within a week of consultation and secure digital record retention (minimum seven (7) years) arrangements.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Documentation, storage and sharing arrangements depend on local pharmacy systems and policy.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm My Health Record upload workflow and patient opt-out handling for each supply.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Upload requirement is stated but the operational process is left to the pharmacy's local workflow.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local escalation pathway for each 'Urgent' destination in the Section G table (regular medical practitioner vs ED vs eye hospital), including the pregnancy instruction to phone ED with notice of urgent medical referral and advising against attending maternity/antenatal appointments while symptomatic.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Destinations are printed but the local contact/booking arrangements are left to the pharmacy's established referral pathways.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm whether patients in rows marked 'Treat: Yes' with an 'Urgent' referral destination may be supplied antivirals by the pharmacist while the urgent referral proceeds, or must be referred without supply.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The document simultaneously marks these rows as treatable and requires urgent referral; the operational rule is not stated.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm how to handle patients previously vaccinated for herpes zoster at eligibility check (row states Treat: Yes with Urgent: GP referral, and confirmatory pathology testing is required for previously vaccinated patients).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The interaction between the urgent GP referral row and ongoing pharmacist management is not explained in the document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local policy on exercising professional discretion and judgement when applying the Practice Standards.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The standard explicitly defers to pharmacist judgement and consultation with the patient, which is a local policy/governance decision.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local definition/escalation for immunocompromised patients (underlying condition examples and medication examples) with choice of 'Urgent: ED or GP', and for disseminated/atypical presentations with 'Urgent: ED'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The table gives example lists ('e.g.') and dual destinations without specifying which destination applies to which patient; local escalation policy must be confirmed.
